articles.summary: Gustavo Gabriel Vieira de Lira e Vitor Bernardino Nabuco formam indiciados por furto qualificado. Imagens do Metrô mostraram a perseguição e queda da vítima, que quebrou costelas.
articles.body:
O ex-vereador do PSD tinha sido vítima de um assalto na Avenida Doutor Arnaldo, na Zona Oeste da capital paulista, na noite de 12 de agosto. Ao perseguir os suspeitos que haviam acabado de levar o aparelho, ele caiu de uma escada, fraturou cinco costelas e teve outros ferimentos.

A ocorrência aconteceu na altura da Estação Clínicas do Metrô. Marco Aurélio estava dentro de um táxi, que teve o vidro quebrado por um membro da "gangue do quebra-vidros".

Os dois criminosos foram identificados graças às câmeras de vigilância da estação, que flagraram tanto a queda do ex-vereador quanto a fuga dos dois suspeitos para dentro da estação.

Os ladrões foram identificados como Gustavo Gabriel Vieira de Lira e Vitor Bernardino Nabuco. Eles formam indiciados por furto qualificado. Imagens do Metrô mostraram a perseguição e queda da vítima, que quebrou cinco costelas. — Foto: Reprodução/SSP

O caso foi investigado pela 2ª Delegacia de Polícia de Investigações sobre Furtos, Roubos e Receptação de Cargas (2ª DISCCPAT), do Departamento Estadual de Investigações Criminais (Deic).

De acordo com a Secretaria da Segurança Pública (SSP), os dois homens suspeitos de envolvimento no crime foram localizados e indiciados.

Eles se chamam Gustavo Gabriel Vieira de Lira e Vitor Bernardino Nabuco . Ambos foram localizados nos respectivos endereços durante o cumprimento dos mandados de prisão expedidos pela Justiça de São Paulo.

Na residência de Gustavo, os policiais apreenderam dois aparelhos celulares. Após consulta aos sistemas policiais, constatou-se que um deles possuía registro de furto, relacionado a ocorrência em 2025.

Diante dessa constatação, ele foi preso em flagrante pelo crime de receptação. Ele também foi indiciado formalmente por furto qualificado no inquérito policial que apura o roubo do celular de Marco Aurélio Cunha.

Gustavo Gabriel Vieira de Lira e Vitor Bernardino Nabuco aparecem na perseguição onde Marco Aurélio Cunha tropeça na escada e quebra cinco costelas. — Foto: Reprodução/SSP

Já no endereço de Vitor Nabuco, os policiais localizaram e apreenderam um aparelho celular e uma blusa que, segundo os elementos reunidos na investigação, teria sido utilizada no dia dos fatos, ocorrido em 12 de agosto de 2026.

Ele também foi indiciado pelo crime de furto qualificado praticado mediante concurso de duas ou mais pessoas e, após os procedimentos de polícia judiciária, foi liberado.

Os celulares apreendidos serão submetidos às providências investigativas e periciais cabíveis. As investigações prosseguem para o completo esclarecimento dos fatos e consolidação dos elementos de prova, segundo a polícia.

Marco Aurélio Cunha foi vítima de um assalto na Avenida Doutor Arnaldo, na Zona Oeste da capital, na noite de 12 de agosto. Ao perseguir o suspeito que havia acabado de levar seu celular, ele caiu de uma escada, fraturou cinco costelas e teve outros ferimentos.

"Eu voltava da Avenida Paulista para a minha casa, em um táxi, na parte de trás. Passando pela Doutor Arnaldo, na altura do metrô, onde tem uma escada do metrô, um sujeito deu um impacto violento no vidro e arrancou o meu celular da minha mão", relatou ele em vídeo feito ainda no hospital.

O comentarista afirmou que, ao perceber que havia sido vítima de um assalto, saiu do carro e começou a correr atrás do homem.

" Ele entrou na escada do metrô, ali do Araçá, do cemitério, e caiu. Talvez isso tenha me dado impulso de correr. Eu acho que é errado, mas na hora você não pensa muito. Caí na escada, bati o tórax, acho que no gradil também, fiz um ferimento na cabeça. Um pneumotórax pequeno, que eu espero que reabsorva sem intervenção cirúrgica. É o caminho, parece que está indo bem", comentou ele, que também é médico.

Apesar dos ferimentos, ele disse que sua recuperação evolui de forma satisfatória e teve alta após quatro dias de internação.

"A gente tem muito policiamento na Paulista, mas nas cercanias a gente tem que ter umas rondas ali para evitar que isso aconteça, porque os pontos que eles fazem isso todo mundo já sabe", apontou a vítima.

Os dois criminosos já tinham sido flagrados quebrando vidros de outros carros no mesmo trecho da Av. Doutor Arnaldo, segundo câmeras de vigilância do local.

articles.title: Can orphan adopted legally be 'returned' years later?
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Can an orphan adopted legally after following all procedures be \"returned\" years later if the adoptive parents are unable to handle the tru.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Can an orphan adopted legally after following all procedures be "returned" years later if the adoptive parents are unable to handle the truant minor or if the child poses a threat to them?The case of one such child, adopted in 2018 by a couple but now proving a handful for the mother, has reached the Delhi high court, which sought the stand of the authorities, reports Abhinav Garg.Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma, during a hearing last week, pointed out that there aren't too many precedents, if any, to shed light on law governing return of a minor in such cases and asked Centre, through Central Adoption Resource Authority, to furnish its stand. HC also issued notice to Child Welfare Committee - Kasturba Niketan Complex at Lajpat Nagar and asked it to respond if the minor can be housed at the facility.Recognising the urgency and importance of the matter, HC asked the authorities to respond by Sept 30. It was hearing a plea filed by the mother of the boy seeking directions to hand over his custody to CARA or any govt organisation or any private organisation, which can also provide all necessary medical care and treatment to the child for which she will bear the expenses to the best of her financial capacity.Explaining her predicament, the woman, through advocate Ali Bin Saif, informed the court that she and her husband adopted the child, then six years old, via CARA in 2018.“It was later discovered that he was intellectually disabled and was indulging in inappropriate behaviour, including aggression, committing theft and was expelled from multiple schools,” Saif submitted, adding that three years after the adoption, the woman lost her husband and is now living with her mother and sister.“The petitioner and her husband adopted the respondent no. 4 (boy) at the age of 6 years and either his medical examination was not conducted in the proper manner or the concerned doctors were not able to detect his illness,” the plea says, adding that the couple admitted him in a school where he behaved inappropriately with a schoolmate. “The petitioner was informed about such incident by the school authority and the boy was expelled from the school.”Highlighting that three aged women are at present grappling with the boy, the petition says that due to his behaviour, petitioner and her old age mother are in constant fear that he will misbehave. The petition adds that he has been expelled from many schools and “due to mental disability, the petitioner is in constant fear that the boy can do anything with her if she stopped him from stealing money or misbehaving”.Seeking the court’s intervention, the mother says that with passage of time the adopted son is “becoming more violent and there is apprehension that he can misbehave... and therefore it is not safe for the petitioner and her mother and her sister.”You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A 17-year-old girl was allegedly gang-raped by three men at Astha Kunj Park near Kalkaji Mandir after the accused allegedly posed as police.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A 17-year-old girl was allegedly gang-raped by three men at Astha Kunj Park near Kalkaji Mandir after the accused allegedly posed as policemen and separated her from her male friend, Delhi Police said.The incident unfolded over a little more than an hour on Sunday, according to the police account.7pm: Darshan at Kalkaji MandirThe girl and her male friend had gone to Kalkaji Mandir for darshan at around 7pm, police said. After visiting the temple, the two entered the nearby Astha Kunj Park through Gate No. 7.7.30pm: Three men allegedly pose as copsWhile the two were inside the park, three men allegedly approached them and claimed to be policemen. The men allegedly separated the girl from her friend and took her towards a secluded area.One of the accused, identified as Asif, allegedly threatened the girl with a firearm and a knife before sexually assaulting her. The other two men also allegedly sexually assaulted her, police said.The three accused subsequently allegedly threatened the girl and her friend.8.45pm: PCR call triggers police actionA PCR call regarding the alleged rape was received at around 8.45pm. The SHO of Amar Colony police station and police staff reached Astha Kunj Park, where they found the girl and her friend.The girl was subsequently medically examined at AIIMS. Police said he fired three rounds despite being asked to surrender.One of the rounds hit head constable Rajesh's bulletproof jacket. articles.title: Inside Scotland's wildcat HQ - 'It's like Big Brother for cats'
articles.summary: The Saving Wildcats partnership is keeping an eye on the latest wildcats being bred in captivity for release into the Cairngorms.
articles.body:
From behind a giant bank of screens in a small windowless room, Estelle Morgan, animal team leader from the Saving Wildcats partnership, is keeping an eye on the latest wildcats being bred in captivity for release into the Cairngorms.

"It's like Big Brother for cats", she says of the 72 cameras being used to watch over the animals in their enclosures.

They are assessing whether they're healthy and have the behavioural potential to survive in the wild.

"We want to know what the cats are actually doing," she says.

"What are they like without us there? she adds. "Are they able to climb? Are they able to pounce? Can they navigate complex structures? Are they active at natural times?"

This year they were even able to capture on camera for the first time a wildcat giving birth.

It is quite a surveillance programme - but it has to be.

They don't want the cats to become comfortable around people and contact is kept to an absolute minimum.

They are also assessing the cats' behaviour ahead of being released: "If we've got some cats which are quite bold does that mean they're more likely to go near roads in the wild, or venture closer to a farm or to human settlements," she says.

Those wildcats have successfully reproduced and the team working on the project are aware of at least 20 wild-born litters to released females since 2024.

There are now plans to reintroduce wildcat populations into other areas in Scotland.

The Cairngorm project has had "an enormous amount of success, but it is only the first step," says NatureScot species project manager Dr Martin Gaywood.

Now he says they need to think big: "Wildcat conservation is really complex. It has all sorts of threats and issues and in order to restore wildcats to the whole of Scotland we need to plan long term and we need to plan at a big scale."

Dr Gaywood is optimistic that with careful planning the translocation of wildcats into other parts of Scotland could happen within years: "It would be great maybe within the next five years to start at least one new project, you never know maybe two," he says.

As well as identifying new release sites, the national strategy will prioritise restoring and reconnecting wildcat habitats to allow the expansion of their range.

In the areas chosen for the eventual translocation of wildcat populations there will be additional microchipping, neutering and vaccination of pet and feral cats to reduce interbreeding.

Dr Helen Senn, head of conservation and science at the Royal Zoological Society of Scotland (RZSS), says climate change is one of the reasons why is it important to identify other areas in which wildcat populations can be reintroduced.

"We have had some really big climate incidents here in the Strath over the last couple of years.

"We've had some major storms and flooding incidents. We've also had, unfortunately, a very significant forest fire in the north of the release area and all of these have the potential to impact the population".

She adds: "The way to be resilient to risk is to have larger population sizes and to have populations present in multiple areas".

They are classed as critically endangered so even once released the wildcats that now roam the Cairngorms are still carefully monitored.

A network of trail cameras - up to 100 at any one time - captures their movements.

The wildcats are also fitted with collars which drop off after around seven to nine months in the wild which emit a signal for a short period of time every day.

Louise Hughes, who is operations manager for the Saving Wildcats partnership, explains that the information they are gathering is invaluable, although not always easy to pick up.

She says the wildcats establishing their new territories: "Might be down a hole, they might be in a tree root, they might have gone for a wander over the mountains."

But the data can help the scientists learn more about the cats' movements and hunting behaviour. It can also help them understand the habitat the wildcats are using.

Scottish Land and Estates has been supportive of the Scottish Wildcat Conservation Action Plan.

Several estates have been actively helping: providing release sites, monitoring the wildcats, recording sightings.

Lots of the information being gathered does come from public sightings.

Louise takes me to the territory on which one wildcat that was recently captured on camera: "The cat that lives in this territory, Sully, is an amazing cat. She was released in 2024 and she has been captured on video swimming across the River Spey."

Wildcats, she says, "never cease to surprise us."

Estelle Morgan points out that wildcats were once widespread throughout the UK.

The work they are doing in the Cairngorms will help inform releases elsewhere in Scotland.

She says the only native cat found in the wild in Britain "deserves to be here, they're part of the landscape."

articles.title: Council plans winter support for vulnerable Tandridge residents
articles.summary: People could be eligible for awards of between £150 to £250, depending on their circumstances.
articles.body:
A Surrey council is poised to set aside £150,000 to support its most vulnerable residents through the winter months.

Tandridge District Council plans to run its winter support scheme for another year, giving eligible residents money to help with essentials and bills.

Councillors on the strategy and resources committee are due to consider the proposals this week, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service .

"Each past scheme has helped nearly 500 households," a report issued ahead of Thursday's meeting says.

Those applying for the support must be a householder aged 16 or over, have their primary residence in the Tandridge District Council area and be struggling to meet their essential short-term needs.

Several categories of residents will be prioritised for aid, including those with dependent children, those with disabilities, pensioners, carers, those at risk of homelessness and victims of domestic abuse.

Council officers will assess any application for support and decide on each case based on "local economic factors and arrangements in place with other agencies".

The report adds the scheme will be fully funded by Tandridge District Council using allocated funds.

Applications would open on 9 November if the renewed programme is approved.

"Awards will not normally exceed £150 for households without children and £250 for households containing children," the report adds.

articles.title: How Shropshire and Worcestershire are dealing with fuel prices
articles.summary: It comes as fuel prices reach their highest since 2022, driven by conflict in the Middle East.
articles.body:
Small businesses are bearing the brunt of rising fuel prices, the owner of a haulage company has said.

Noel Lewis, who runs Lewis Light Haulage & Storage in Stourport-on-Severn, Worcestershire, said he was having to absorb thousands of pounds a month in extra costs due to the price of fuel.

His comments come as fuel prices - driven by conflict in the Middle East - reach their highest point since 2022 , with diesel averaging at £1.92 per litre according to the RAC.

A Treasury spokesperson said the government continued "to protect the British people and businesses from this crisis".

"This means drivers benefit from the extension of the 5p fuel duty cut, with diesel 11p per litre cheaper until the end of the year than it would have been compared to plans inherited from the previous government," they added.

Hauliers would also benefit from a 12-month road tax "holiday", the spokesperson said.

With six vehicles run by his company, Lewis said he was now facing around £1,200 in extra fuel costs per week.

Smaller businesses like his, he said, were now struggling to compete with larger firms with "bigger buying power on their fuel".

"They have the economies of scale working in their favour [...] if you put your prices up somebody might come in and be able to suffer that cost for a few weeks, just to knock you out the game," he said.

Lewis explained that he and his wife had been forced to take wage cuts in order to keep money in the business and avoid passing price increases onto customers.

"With businesses, you want to keep custom coming back to you so you do not want to put your prices too high," he said.

According to the RAC, the cost of filling up a vehicle is now at a similar level to when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The US-Israel war with Iran has severely disrupted the production and transportation of oil across the region, with the effects felt worldwide.

It is not just businesses being impacted - individual drivers are also seeing soaring prices at the pumps. Susan Parkes from Telford drives a diesel car and said the prices she pays had become "extortionate."

"We went on holiday and we had to put in an extra £20 in the tank which, brought us up to about £120," Parkes added

"You have to cut your cloth accordingly. Where you are used to having a treat, you have got to think about your meals and shopping [because of money spent on fuel]."

Katie Woollacott, also from Telford, said she used an app to find the cheapest fuel and often drove outside the town to find lower prices.

"Personally, I would rather travel about 20 minutes to 30 minutes going either towards Birmingham or Whitchurch, because it's like 20p cheaper," she said.

"I stopped to refill the other day and it cost me about almost £70 for my 1.6 litre Mini, so it's definitely a jump as I do not normally spend over 50.

A government spokesperson said they would "tackle the cost of living to make life's essentials affordable again and bring back hope", and pointed towards the Fuel Finder service which uses data to help drivers find the cheapest fuel near them.

articles.title: 'Shocking' 1940s and 50s litter found on west Dorset beaches
articles.summary: Litter pickers found a World War Two tin lid and a 50-year-old medicine bottle from Colombia.
articles.body:
A World War Two-era plaster tin lid and a 50-year-old plastic medicine bottle from Colombia are among the items collected from beaches by litter pickers.

Weymouth and Portland Marine Litter Project is marking its fifth year of reducing litter and pollution on the Dorset coast and has been sharing some of its most surprising finds.

The charity runs several initiatives, including cleaning the coastline between Osmington and Chickerell.

Co-founder Dave Taylor, who researches some of the more interesting pieces of litter, said it had been "shocking" to see how long plastic survived.

The medicine bottle, believed to be from the 1970s, was found on Chesil Beach in 2025.

It bears the words "venta bajo formula medico" - sale by prescription only - and an address in Cali, Colombia.

Other items found include a Cooltan sun cream tube, an Odorono deodorant bottle and a Quix washing-up liquid bottle - all believed to date back to the 1950s and 60s.

Taylor uses reverse image searches, AI and archive material to help trace the origins of unusual or old-looking items.

He said: "It's quite interesting. Things like the deodorant bottle, you can find adverts and archive photos. With the washing-up bottle, the brand only lasted a limited time.

"The sun tan lotion was found by a metal detectorist. Cooltan was made in Brixton in the 1950s, then they closed after that, so it's been on Weymouth beach all that time."

The oldest items Taylor has found are glass bottles dating back to Victorian times.

During its five-year history, the marine litter project has saved more than 20 tonnes of waste from the sea.

Its carries out litter picking and organises projects such as fishing gear and crabbing line recycling, a library of discarded beach toys, as well as by recycling washed-up nets, rope and rigid plastics.

articles.title: Bihar molestation case: India outrage after assault of teen girl and her friend in Jamui
articles.summary: Three minors were arrested after videos capturing the assault went viral in India, sparking anger.
articles.body:
A video showing a teenaged girl being sexually assaulted and her male friend beaten by a group of men in India's Bihar state has sparked widespread outrage.

The school students, both minors, were stopped in Jamui district on 19 September. Footage shared widely online shows them surrounded and repeatedly pleading to be allowed to leave.

The boy is seen being slapped and pulled by his collar, while the girl is touched inappropriately and, in another clip, carried away by a man as the boy tries to intervene.

Three accused, also minors, have been arrested in connection with the assault. A special investigation team has been set up to catch the other suspects.

The disturbing footage has prompted anger over the harassment of the two teenagers and renewed a wider debate about the safety of women and girls in Bihar, as well as questions over the response of state authorities.

The outrage intensified after Bihar minister Shravan Kumar said that "sporadic incidents keep happening" and that the government was keeping a watch on them.

"The world is not entirely free of crime," he said, adding that those responsible would not be allowed to escape and would face strict action.

Umesh Kushwaha, of the governing Janata Dal (United), also faced criticism after referring to such cases as "isolated incidents" and contrasting the government's record with that of the previous RJD administration.

Kushwaha later said his remarks had been "distorted and misrepresented" and promised action against those responsible.

Police said the incident took place around 19:00 local time [13:30 GMT] on Saturday, but it came to light on Monday after the video of the assault went viral.

The teenagers, both students of 10th standard, attended the same coaching institute and had gone to the area to take photographs after their classes, according to police.

Jamui police chief Bishwajeet Dayal said neither of them had initially reported the incident - officers began investigating after the video circulated widely online and traced the pair using the registration number of a vehicle visible in the footage.

Their statements were subsequently recorded and a case was registered following a written complaint from the girl.

A case has been registered under India's stringent Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, or Pocso.

Police have also invoked sections of India's criminal code covering assault or criminal force against a woman with intent to outrage her modesty, assault or criminal force with intent to disrobe, and acts carried out with a common intention.

Senior police officer KS Anupam said three minors had been arrested and that investigators had established the involvement of two other people.

Police have also begun action against 32 social media accounts accused of circulating footage in which the teenagers could be identified, she added.

The shocking nature of the assault has provoked outrage online, with many social media users expressing horror and questioning why a group of men believed they had the right to confront two teenagers for being together.

Some characterised the incident as an extreme form of "moral policing", while others tagged Bihar police and demanded strict action against the harassers.

Shreyasi Singh, a Bihar minister and legislator from Jamui, told NDTV news channel the incident had brought "shame to society".

Singh, a former international-level sport shooter, said women in Bihar were advancing in many areas but concerns about their safety persisted.

She called for the remaining suspects to be arrested quickly and for strict action against those responsible.

Opposition leaders, meanwhile, have seized on the case to question the state government's record on women's safety.

Rahul Gandhi, MP and senior leader of India's main opposition Congress party, described the footage as "deeply disturbing" and said the incident reflected a patriarchal "belief that men could police a girl's body, movements and choices".

"This is not culture. It is patriarchy," Gandhi wrote on X (formerly Twitter).

Tejashwi Yadav, the opposition leader in Bihar, said the incident had left him "deeply ashamed" and accused the government of failing to ensure the safety of women and girls in the state.

Members of Bihar's governing coalition have rejected the opposition's wider criticism of the state's law-and-order record and said those responsible for the attack would face strict action.

India's National Commission for Women has also intervened, calling for all those involved to be identified and arrested and for an impartial investigation.

The commission has asked for a report from Bihar police and urged authorities to prevent further sharing of the video clips to protect the girl's identity and privacy.

The Bihar State Women's Commission has also sought information from district authorities about the action being taken in the case.

articles.title: Northampton divers clear fly-tipped waste from River Nene
articles.summary: Divers from the Northampton Scuba School team up with other local organisations for a clean-up.
articles.body:
A team of divers from Northampton Scuba School arranged a six-hour clean-up of the River Nene in Northampton.

They collected two old shopping trolleys, a milk churn, a number of car tyres, an old bike, a drill and charger.

The event on Saturday 19 September was organised alongside Northampton Active and Northampton Rowing Club, with the aim of clearing as much rubbish from the river as possible.

Organisers at Northampton Scuba School said they are committed to removing waste from the River Nene on a regular basis and plan to return in the coming months.

A spokesperson for Northampton Scuba School said: "It was an amazing day and a brilliant example of what can be achieved through teamwork, support and a shared commitment to our local environment.

We are incredibly proud of everyone who took part and are looking forward to continuing this important work."

The clean-up team was loaned two canoes from Northampton Active, which were used to support the divers.

The Northampton Canoe and Kayak Club also provided a ladder to help divers get in and out of the water safely.

Anyone not diving was invited to join the litter-picking team along the riverbank, where waste was also collected.

Organisers said the amount of waste collected shows that there's a lot of work to do, and the team will now support regular dives throughout the year.

articles.title: Sheffield's Graves Gallery to close ahead of library refurbishment
articles.summary: The Graves Gallery collection will be moved to a temporary location next year.
articles.body:
A Sheffield arts venue that has showcased work by Pablo Picasso and Andy Warhol is to close next month ahead of a major refurbishment project.

Graves Gallery, located above Sheffield Central Library, will close at the end of October, with its contents housed at an interim base before going on show at a temporary space in the Heart of the City next year.

It comes under plans to "breathe new life" into the Grade II* listed building, which houses the gallery and library, as well as the city archives.

Sheffield Museums chief Kim Streets said: "It is a farewell not a goodbye... we want to see the (library) building receive investment so it's fit for the next century... we are excited about that."

Graves Gallery is situated on the third floor of Central Library and has been a feature of the city's cultural life since 1934.

Earlier this year, the gallery was forced to close when problems with the heating system saw several artworks being removed for fear of damage.

Streets said there was always a plan to move out when the redevelopment started in earnest, but after Sheffield City Council confirmed the heating system could not be fixed, the move came earlier than expected.

The council said the move would help to speed up the next stage of its plans to redevelop the library.

Streets said the library was an "important part of living in a city, people will miss it... and we will continue to work closely with the library to signpost people and keep it (Graves Gallery) in people's minds".

The temporary location for the collection has yet to be confirmed, but the council said it would have street-level access.

Sheffield Museums said it had been working closely with the council on its 18-month feasibility study which is due to be presented and considered by the council in the coming months.

articles.title: Daisy Edgar-Jones: Fields of Fermanagh prepared actress for Sense and Sensibility
articles.summary: The actress, whose mum is from County Down, recalls long childhood summers in Northern Ireland.
articles.body:
Actress Daisy Edgar-Jones is no stranger to Ireland, having spent five months in the country filming hit drama Normal People which was released in 2020.

But it was actually fields in County Fermanagh, where some of her family live, that helped her prepare for the role of beloved character Elinor Dashwood in Jane Austen's Sense and Sensibility, some 20 years before.

Her mother is from County Down and Edgar-Jones, now 28, spent her childhood roaming the Northern Irish countryside.

"I remember big long summers when I was very young in Fermanagh in the fields which definitely helped with my Sense and Sensibility journey because I was doing a lot of the similar wandering around, with not much to do, under the big sky and I love being here," she said.

"I always feel so welcome and the people are incredible."

Sense and Sensibility was published in 1811 and has been adapted many times, but the 1995 adaptation starring Kate Winslet, Emma Thompson, Alan Rickman and Hugh Grant is perhaps the best known.

The Austen novel centres around a relatable story of sisterhood and romance, mainly between Elinor Dashwood (Edgar-Jones) and Marianne (Esmé Creed-Miles).

The Dashwood family is left penniless after the death of their father and the two older sisters are in search of a husband as they are forced to leave their home and move to the modest Barton Cottage.

The film was made by production companies Focus Features and Working Title.

Edgar-Jones is surrounded by Irish actresses in the film, with Irish star Caitriona Balfe playing her mother Mrs Dashwood, Fiona Shaw playing Mrs Jennings and Hamnet's Bodhi Rae Breathnach playing the Dashwoods' youngest sister, Margaret.

Balfe has often appeared on screens in recent years, mostly in her roles in Outlander and Belfast, alongside Jamie Dornan.

Having grown up in a family of seven in the village of Tydavnet, County Monaghan, Balfe said starring in the film reminded her of her own childhood.

"There was a lot of that sisterly dynamic that I recognised," she said.

"This is one of the beautiful things about this film is watching the richness of this family.

"One of the words that kept coming to me was the resilience of them - even though they were destitute financially, what you see when they go to Barton is actually this blossoming, because they have each other."

She said it was an "amazing" time in Ireland for art.

"I'm so proud to be Irish and it's such an amazing time in Ireland right now for all the incredible art that is being produced here and to be able to bring this film here is really special," she said.

Balfe said she speaks with her husband about moving back to Ireland "all the time".

"You never know, it might be in the future."

Sense and Sensibility is in cinemas from 25 September.

articles.title: Unexpected UK borrowing surge adds to pre-Budget pressure on chancellor
articles.summary: Borrowing was higher than expected in August as inflation piles pressure on the government ahead of the Budget.
articles.body:
An unexpected surge in government borrowing in August, driven by persistently higher inflation, has added to pressure on Chancellor John Healey as he prepares to deliver his first Budget at the end of October.

Borrowing - the difference between tax receipts and government spending - was £18.3bn in August, almost a fifth higher than the year before, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.

That figure was £3.5bn more than official forecasters expected.

Inflation rose to its highest rate in five months in August in the UK, driven up by higher petrol and diesel prices.

Although tax receipts were higher in August compared with a year ago, spending on public services, benefits, and other costs grew more as the pace of price rises increased.

The interest the government is paying on its debt rose to £8.8bn, its highest August level since records began in 1997.

The cost of servicing that debt comes as the government is under pressure to spend more on defence and cost-of-living support to households, said Martin Beck, chief economist at WPI Strategy.

He said it was important not to "overinterpret a single month given the volatility in the numbers", but added that there were some "concerning elements".

He said the cost of paying the interest on government debt is likely to rise in the coming months.

While the figures were an "unwelcome setback", Beck said the government tends to look at the OBR's medium-term fiscal forecast - so what it expects for the public finances three years into the future.

"But even there, the chancellor's got problems," he said. "The cost of that interest has gone up. That's going to feed through into more borrowing."

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) warned that spending on debt interest is "a worryingly large share of overall government spending and has been pushed up" since the last official forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).

Research economist Nick Ridpath said: "Both higher borrowing costs and higher inflation make life harder for a chancellor who is looking to bring down borrowing and to spend more on government priorities."

About a quarter of the interest paid on UK public sector debt is linked to the Retail Prices Index, a measure of inflation which tends to be a higher rate than the Consumer Prices Index measure used to calculate the UK's headline rate.

Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said it is a "dismal backdrop for the autumn Budget, with the government once again borrowing more than expected".

She said the figures raise the likelihood of many of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's policy ambitions being "reined in or delayed to avoid big tax hikes and/or a backlash in the markets".

Gregory also warned that, with the economy weakening, the government is likely to continue borrowing more than expected.

Emma Reynolds, chief secretary to the Treasury, said that the UK has "huge potential" for economic growth, but only with "fiscal discipline" from the government.

"At a time when debt interest costs billions of pounds that could otherwise be spent on improving lives, we must always know where the money is coming from to pay for public services," she said.

She added that the government is committed to its fiscal rules "with a buffer against uncertainty".

However, Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the Labour government had "lost control of the public finances" by overshooting the OBR's forecasts.

"Only the Conservatives will make the tough choices on welfare and public spending to get Britain's finances under control," he said.

Economists think the chancellor may have to find £15bn, perhaps through tax rises, to do this and meet the government's self-imposed spending rules.

Inflation - the pace of price rises - has been above target, and putting pressure on the UK economy.

Consumer price inflation rose to its highest rate in five months in the year to August, running at 3.1%, pushed up in part by the fallout from the US-Israel war in Iran.

articles.title: US’s 5th-gen stealth fighter F-35 to take part in IAF’s multinational exercise 'Tarang Shakti'

Japanese General Takehiro Morita, Chief of Staff of the Japan Air Self-Defense Force, became the first air force chief of any Asian country to fly in India’s made-in-India fighter aircraft LCA or Tejas when he and IAF chief Air Chief Marshal AP Singh last Sunday participated in a formation sortie in Jodhpur as part of the ‘Exercise Veer Guardian-2026’. General Takehiro Morita flew in a Tejas twin-seater trainer aircraft, with Gp Capt I Samrat, Commanding Officer of the Tejas Squadron, as the captain.During a joint press meet last Sunday, Japanese General Morita said, “I will remember it not only as a truly valuable experience, but also as a powerful symbol of trust, confidence, and friendship. articles.title: A Florida artist spent decades turning his property into a maze of sculptures, strange buildings and gardens; after years behind closed gates, his family is reopening the Warlock House Halloween tradition
articles.summary: US News: Lewis VanDercar spent decades transforming his property in Wesley Chapel, Florida, into an unusual space filled with sculptures, artwork, gardens, unc.
articles.body: Lewis VanDercar spent decades transforming his property in Wesley Chapel, Florida, into an unusual space filled with sculptures, artwork, gardens, unconventional buildings and other creations. It is now being reopened for the first time, reviving the property's Haloween tradition, Wesley Chapel Record reorted.The artist became known locally as the 'Warlock of Wesley Chapel' because of the distinctive property he created. His connection with Halloween also goes back to the 1970s, when he lived there with his family and neighbours were invited over for stories, costumes, tricks and treats.The Warlock Family Spookfest will be held on October 3 at The Warlock House Enchantment in Wesley Chapel. The family-friendly event will allow visitors to explore parts of the property while taking part in games, crafts, storytelling, live entertainment and other themed activities.The event is also bringing back a part of the Halloween tradition associated with VanDercar. Children attending the Spookfest will receive Warlock Apprentice Passports and can collect stamps at different themed stations. The activities include pirates, mermaids, herbology, bubbles, carnival games, broom decorating and storytelling.How Warlock House took shapeVanDercar moved to the Wesley Chapel area in 1973 and bought eight acres of land. He later built a dome-shaped, ivy-covered home that was designed to resemble a cave. Over the years, he filled the property with concrete sculptures, gardens, artwork and unusual architecture.His work was not limited to his own property. Before moving to Wesley Chapel, VanDercar drew Popeye cartoons from a Miami studio in the late 1930s. He later served in the merchant marines during World War II and worked as an aircraft engineer before making a living through painting and sculpting.Among his other works were a gorilla’s lair for Monkey Jungle in South Dade and a giant dragon for a park on Merritt Island.The unusual nature of his work also led to questions about whether he was a 'crazy' artist or a genius. In his December 1988 Miami Herald obituary, VanDercar responded to the description by saying, “I'm both. I think us geniuses should be modest.”The property he created eventually became closely associated with his identity as the 'Warlock of Wesley Chapel'. His grandson Bobby VanDercar now operates VanDercar Studio, a painting business in the Tampa area. The studio’s website describes Lewis VanDercar’s concrete sculptures as having transformed the Wesley Chapel property into an artistic landmark.Halloween tradition returnsAccording to the Wesley Chapel Record, a neighbour named Jeff Daniels recalled that VanDercar “would invite us neighbor kids over at Halloween to tell us stories.”The new Spookfest is built around a similar family-friendly approach. Rather than focusing on frightening visitors, the event will offer themed activities that children can explore around the property.Children will use their Warlock Apprentice Passports as they move between activities. They can collect stamps at the different stations and receive a special prize after completing their adventure.The event will also include games, crafts, live entertainment, food vendors and other activities. Families can attend in costumes, although the organisers describe the experience as playful rather than scary.According to The Laker Lutz News, the festival will take place from 2 to 6 pm. on October 3 at The Warlock House Enchantment, located at 25950 Queen Sago Place in Wesley Chapel.Admission is $15 for adults and $10 for children aged 10 and older. Children younger than 10 can attend for free.Statuary tours planned in OctoberThe Halloween event is not the only opportunity for people to see the property. The Warlock House Enchantment will also offer statuary tours on Tuesdays and Fridays throughout October.The tours are scheduled for 7 pm and 10 pm and will give visitors an opportunity to see the sculptures and other creations on the historic property.The opening marks a change for a place that had largely remained behind closed gates. articles.title: In 2021, researchers examining a circular ridge in China’s forest found shocked quartz, melted granite and glass, confirming the 1.85-kilometre Yilan feature as a meteor crater
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Researchers have identified the Yilan feature in China's Heilongjiang Province as a meteorite impact crater, revealing shocking geological evidence such as shocked quartz and melted granite. This discovery sheds light on the Earth's history and highlights the importance of hidden geological formations in understanding past cosmic events.
articles.body: The Lesser Xingan mountain range in northeastern China is covered in deep forest, a type of landscape that can conceal geological characteristics so well that even remarkable landforms may go undiscovered by scientists for generations. Locals in the Heilongjiang Province's city of Yilan had long been aware of an odd circular ridge in the forest that they called Quanshan, or circle mountain ridge. However, they had no reason to believe it was anything other than a peculiar feature of the area. This peaceful forest feature was actually the remnant of a cataclysmic collision from Earth's distant past, as discovered after a rigorous drilling operation and a new examination of satellite photos.The origin of the ridge first came under suspicion in about 2021, when researchers re-examined satellite images showing its distinctive, almost horseshoe-shaped outline, a telltale indicator to geologists who study impact formations. The southern part of the rim was missing altogether, but the remaining arc rose as high as 150 metres above the crater floor, unusually well preserved for a feature of its age. NASA Earth Observatory later shared Landsat 8 satellite imagery from October 8, 2021, showing the scalloped edge of the crater highlighted by autumn foliage, a striking visual record of the same shape that had first raised researchers' suspicions.Drilling for evidence beneath the treesJust having the right shape wasn't enough to prove it was from an impact, so a study team led by Ming Chen of the Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry at the Chinese Academy of Sciences dug 438 metres into the core of the structure to see what lay beneath the forest floor. The core they brought out had a dramatic story to tell. Underneath more than a hundred metres of old lake sediment lay a thick layer of broken granite, with evident traces of tremendous shock.The scientists identified shocked quartz crystals with the parallel planar deformation patterns that only occur under the severe pressures of a hypervelocity impact and pockets of melted granite, glass riddled with gas bubble holes and teardrop-shaped glass fragments that had clearly cooled from a molten state. Their full findings were later documented in Meteoritics and Planetary Science, the journal that carried the original study.The evidence combined to leave few options. Normal volcanic or erosional processes simply cannot produce shocked quartz with these particular crystal orientations, a fingerprint that geologists consider close to solid evidence of a meteorite strike. The granite of the bedrock itself is around 200 million years old, laid down in the Early Jurassic.An old planet with a new scarRadiocarbon dating of charcoal and lacustrine silt in the crater fill constrains the impact to between around 47,000 and 53,000 years ago. The 1.85-kilometre-wide Yilan crater is the largest confirmed impact feature on Earth younger than 100,000 years. The young age of the crater is one reason this find is so noteworthy. About 190 impact craters have been confirmed worldwide, but most are so badly eroded or buried that it’s hard or impossible to recreate specifics of the original strike. Ironically, the same thick forest cover that kept Yilan hidden for so long makes its survival more surprising still, since most craters this old have long since been worn away by exactly this kind of dense vegetation and root growth. The Astrophysics Data System, maintained by Harvard and the Smithsonian, also archives a detailed abstract of the study.The find is only the second confirmed impact crater ever discovered in China, after a previous discovery in Liaoning province. Scientists think the impactor was about 100 metres wide, and because the crater is relatively young, it is probable that anyone living in Siberia and northern Asia at the time would have seen it, despite there being no direct record of it. It’s a reminder that, even on a world as well-mapped as ours, forests and far-flung landscapes may hide secrets of truly cosmic proportions.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Space-age warfare: DRDO develops a more powerful laser that can take out drones at 5 km
articles.summary: News News: India is moving to take its indigenous directed-energy weapon capability from trials to production, with the Defence Research and Development Organisa.
articles.body: India is moving to take its indigenous directed-energy weapon capability from trials to production, with the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) set to seek an industry partner within the next six months for its 30kW-class counter-drone laser weapon. The move comes as militaries increasingly look at directed-energy weapons as a way to deal with the growing threat posed by large numbers of low-cost drones and unmanned aerial vehicles.The truck-mounted 30kW laser system is designed primarily to counter drone swarms, fixed-wing UAVs and surveillance sensors at ranges of up to 5 km. According to DRDO, final trials of the system were completed in August 2025 and the technology has now been demonstrated. The requirement for such systems has become more pressing after recent conflicts, including Operation Sindoor in May 2025, when drones were extensively used by both sides. Pakistan used relatively cheap drones for probing and surveillance missions, including attempts to locate Indian air-defence positions and force the expenditure of expensive interceptors. This has highlighted a basic problem in modern air defence: using a costly missile to destroy a relatively inexpensive drone can quickly become unsustainable when attacks involve large numbers of targets.Lasers offer a different approach. Travelling at the speed of light, a high-energy laser beam can engage a target instantly, without the flight time associated with missiles and at a much cheaper cost per shot. As long as sufficient electrical power is available, the system does not face the traditional ammunition constraints of kinetic weapons. This makes Directed Energy Weapons (DEW) particularly relevant against drone swarms and other relatively slow aerial targets.India is also developing smaller laser systems. The 2kW DEW is already in production through Adani, Astra and Bharat Electronics Limited, while the 10kW version has cleared the key acceptance of necessity stage and 10-12 systems have been ordered. Larsen & Toubro and BEL have been selected as development-cum-production partners for the 10kW system, which is intended to engage targets up to 2 km.The 30kW system represents a significant step up in capability and is part of India's wider effort to develop a layered air-defence architecture under Project Sudarshan Chakra. DRDO has also been working towards higher-power 50kW and 100kW-class systems. The global race in directed-energy weapons is already underway. The US has tested and deployed laser-based counter-drone systems, Israel is developing its 100kW-class Iron Beam, while China has showcased systems such as Silent Hunter and LY-1. Russia is also among the countries pursuing DEW technologies.DRDO is increasingly looking to industry for production and routine engineering work while concentrating on core technologies. The 30kW programme will therefore be an important test of India's ability to move advanced defence research from the laboratory and trials range into the hands of the armed forces. The larger objective is to add another layer to India's air-defence network, combining missiles, guns and electronic warfare along with directed-energy weapons. In a battlespace where drones can arrive in large numbers and at relatively low cost, the ability to defeat them without continually expending expensive interceptors could become an important part of future air defence.

articles.title: Sri Lankan court to deliver verdict on deadly Easter bombings
articles.summary: Co-ordinated suicide attacks killed 270 people across several churches and hotels in Colombo in 2019.
articles.body:
A Sri Lankan court is set to rule on Naufer Moulavi, who is accused of masterminding the Easter bomb attacks that killed 270 people and injured more than 500 in 2019.

Twenty-three others will also receive verdicts for their involvement in planning and carrying out the co-ordinated suicide bombings.

The attacks on several locations including several churches holding Easter mass and three luxury hotels was the deadliest attack Sri Lanka had seen since the end of its civil war in 2009.

The associates and relatives of nine suicide bombers are among those facing more than 23,000 charges , including murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism and possessing firearms.

The prosecution had named Moulavi as the main organiser of the attacks, and had submitted what they said was a voluntary confession to the court where he had admitted his role.

The court accepted the confession. However, Moulavi later told the three-judge bench hearing the case that he was not shown what he was signing and rejected the allegations against him.

More than 2,300 people gave evidence for the prosecution.

There were also 2,076 pieces of evidence, including explosives, swords and firearms.

In the wake of the attacks, Sri Lankan authorities pointed to a "major intelligence lapse". Its parliament heard that a tip-off from India about the attacks was not properly shared with the authorities.

In 2023, the Supreme Court ordered former president Maithripala Sirisena to pay millions in compensation to the victims of the bombings, after finding him responsible for national security failures that led to the attacks.

Last month, two former senior officials were sentenced to death for criminal negligence that led to the bombings. Death sentences are usually commuted to life in prison in Sri Lanka due to a decades-old moratorium on executions.

For years, Sri Lankans have held regular demonstrations demanding justice for the victims of the Easter attacks.

The verdict on Tuesday comes as a separate investigation on former intelligence chief Suresh Sallay is under way. Sallay is accused of orchestrating the bombings with Islamist extremists.

The allegations echo those aired in a 2023 documentary by British broadcaster Channel 4, which heard whistleblower testimony claiming the attacks were allowed to happen to boost the popularity of the Rajapaksa family, which long dominated Sri Lankan politics.

Sallay, who was arrested in February, denies the allegations. Former president Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was elected months after the 2019 attacks, with a campaign of tackling Islamist extremism has also denied the allegations.

Rajapaksa, who has been banned from leaving the country, has asked the court to prevent his potential arrest in connection with the ongoing investigations.

articles.title: In 2023, archaeologists using Cold War satellite images found 396 previously unrecorded Roman forts across Syria and Iraq, challenging an old theory about the empire’s eastern frontier
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 2023, Cold War satellite images revealed 396 previously unknown Roman forts across Syria and Iraq, challenging long-held ideas about Rome’s eastern frontier
articles.body: For over a century, the narrative of the eastern frontier of the Roman Empire was based almost solely on the observations of a single French priest flying a biplane during World War One across the Middle Eastern deserts. Based on aerial surveys conducted in the 1920s and 1930s, Father Antoine Poidebard concluded that the 116 fortified buildings dispersed throughout the area formed a defensive line that ran roughly north to south, creating a permanent military border between Rome and her eastern adversaries. Even as more potent techniques for observing the ancient landscape finally became available, generations of historians generally accepted that interpretation.An unlikely source, declassified satellite images from the Cold War, initially collected for military intelligence objectives rather than archaeology, challenged the frontier theory Poidebard had proposed decades earlier. Dartmouth College archaeologist Jesse Casana and colleagues leveraged imagery from the American CORONA and HEXAGON satellite programmes, acquired between 1960 and 1986 and made publicly available decades after being captured for reconnaissance at the height of Cold War tensions. The images are from before much rapid urbanisation, agricultural growth and decades of conflict in the region; thus, they preserve a depiction of the environment far closer to its ancient state than anything seen in recent satellite shots.Thousands of images, hundreds of fortsThe team subdivided their study zone, a roughly 300,000 square kilometre swathe of the northern Fertile Crescent running from western Syria into northwestern Iraq, into manageable grid squares and visually analysed more than 2,000 satellite photographs for the distinctive square or rectangular imprints of Roman fortifications. Of the 116 forts originally identified by Poidebard, the team could only find 38 in the satellite picture, showing how much of the historic landscape had already been wiped out by decades of current land use change. Using those proven sites as a reference point, the team then combed through that imagery at a finer grid resolution, ultimately screening more than 10,000 probable archaeological features across the full study zone, then trimmed the list to 396 previously unrecorded forts or fort-like structures based on uniform parameters for size and shape.It turned out that the distribution of these newly recognised forts told a remarkably different story than the one Poidebard had proposed. Instead of a defensive line running north to south, the constructions extend far to the east and west, connecting the city of Mosul on the Tigris River with Aleppo in western Syria. That pattern suggested the forts were never intended to be an inflexible military barrier dividing Rome from hostile land to the east but instead functioned more like waypoints supporting trade caravans, troop movements and communication across a fluid frontier zone shared with Parthian and later Sasanian powers. The journal Antiquity has published the full findings.A record that vanished, saved barely in timeWhat makes the discovery particularly remarkable is how much of this material has since vanished altogether from the visible landscape. Many of the forts indicated in the older satellite imagery are nowhere to be seen in present-day shots, having been destroyed or buried under decades of urban expansions, reservoir construction, agricultural expansion and the physical damage inflicted by regional conflict. The declassified imagery utilised in this study forms part of the wider Atlas Project, an open access internet resource that has made thousands of Cold War era satellite photographs available to scholars investigating ancient landscapes across the Middle East and beyond.The research substantially changes long-held notions about how the Roman Empire administered its eastern edge, revealing a frontier far more porous and financially connected than the constructed wall-like barrier that historians had envisaged for over a century. It also points to the growing value of using military intelligence archives for historical research, as imagery taken to monitor Soviet military installations has instead provided an irreplaceable view of a vanished world of antiquity, recorded just before so much of it disappeared forever under the sands and cities of the modern Middle East.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2014, a fire-damaged 1967 Ferrari 330 GTS emerged from decades in a Pennsylvania garage and sold for $2.06 million
articles.summary: US News: A 1967 Ferrari 330 GTS had spent 44 years in a Pennsylvania garage after an engine fire before it was offered at auction in Scottsdale, Arizona. Goodi.
articles.body: A 1967 Ferrari 330 GTS had spent 44 years in a Pennsylvania garage after an engine fire before it was offered at auction in Scottsdale, Arizona. Gooding & Company sold the car in January 2014; the winning bid reached $1.875 million, and the final price was $2,062,500 with the buyer's premium. The car had not been restored and still carried the scars of decades of storage, including damage from the fire that had taken it off the road in the first place.The fire stopped the Ferrari in 1969The Ferrari was sold new through Luigi Chinetti Motors in Greenwich, Connecticut, and was bought by Dr. Samuel Scher. According to contemporary reporting, Scher drove the car for about 20,000 miles during its first two years before an engine fire ended its time on the road. The damaged Ferrari was sold at a Motor Insurance Company auction in 1969, and its second owner bought it but never completed the repairs. Instead, the car went into storage in Pennsylvania and stayed there for the next 44 years.By the time it reached Gooding's Scottsdale auction, it was not a restored classic that was being presented in showroom condition; instead, it was a largely untouched example that still showed the effects of the fire and decades of storage. AutoWeek reported before the sale that the Ferrari had been sitting in a barn for 44 years and did not run.One of only a small number builtPininfarina designed the body, while Ferrari fitted the car with a 3,967cc V12 that produced 300 horsepower, and Gooding described the auction car as the fifth of only 99 examples built and identified it as chassis 9343. The car had been stored for decades, and its engine-fire damage remained, yet its originality was part of what made it attractive to collectors.Gooding's auction description noted that the Ferrari had fewer than 23,000 miles from new, retained its matching numbers and had remained under single-family ownership for more than 40 years. The auction house presented it as a candidate for a concours-quality restoration rather than a finished example. The car's condition also showed a shift in how collectors viewed unrestored vehicles, since an untouched car could retain a separate appeal because its condition preserved evidence of its history rather than being valuable only after a complete mechanical and cosmetic rebuild.The barn find crossed the $2 million markThe Ferrari went onto the Gooding & Company auction block in Scottsdale on January 18, 2014. The winning bid was $1.875 million before the buyer's premium, and produced a final sale price of $2,062,500. Gooding subsequently described the sale as a world auction record for a Ferrari 330 GTS at the time, and its 2014 auction report listed the car among the sale's million-dollar vehicles and recorded the final price of $2,062,500.The Ferrari had gone from an engine fire in 1969 to decades of obscurity and then to a multimillion-dollar auction result without being restored first. Its 44-year wait in a Pennsylvania garage became inseparable from the car's provenance, while the damaged engine remained a physical record of the event that had taken it off the road.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Eleven injured in shooting outside Turkish school
articles.summary: Footage appears to show a male in the area carrying a firearm, while officials say the attacker has been captured.
articles.body:
Eleven people have been injured in a shooting outside a high school in Turkey, with police detaining a 15-year-old male suspect.

Two people were left in critical conditions after a gunman opened fire before fleeing on Tuesday morning

It happened at the Inci Uzmez Vocational and Technical Anatolian High School in the western province of Manisa, with the injured reportedly all students.

The suspect's mother, father, and grandfather - who reportedly owned the weapon - have also been detained, according to the country's justice minister Akın Gürlek.

It is the third school shooting in Turkey this year and comes as the government continues to grapple with how to address the recent spate of violence.

CCTV footage appeared to show the suspect walking through empty streets checking a shotgun, which is clearly visible. He is casually dressed and appears unhurried.

Later footage showed the apparent suspect, who is reportedly a student at the school, running from the scene with the weapon still in hand.

The motive behind the attack was not immediately clear.

According to Turkish law, the teenager is required to appear before a court before being officially arrested.

In a statement, Turkey's education ministry said the incident had "deeply saddened our nation, and our educational community in particular".

It said that three national investigators from the ministry had been sent to Manisa.

Two deadly school shootings in April caused outrage in Turkey and led to new security measures for the 2026-2027 academic year, including tighter gun controls.

Before then, the country did not have a history of school shootings.

In an attack in Kahramanmaras, a 14-year-old killed nine students aged 10 and 11, and one teacher. The gunman died at the scene.

articles.title: Spain battles climate change on several fronts
articles.summary: A summer of wildfires and heatwaves underlines the threats to the country's economy.
articles.body:
In a small green meadow in the Gredos mountains, west of Madrid, a couple of dozen cows belonging to Juan Ángel Izquierdo and his family are grazing. The only noise is the gentle clang of the bells around the animals' necks.

This would be an idyllic scene were it not for the blackened pine and oak trees all around, the legacy of a devastating recent wildfire.

"It was immense, I've never seen anything like it," says Izquierdo, whose family have been farming here for 200 years.

The fire, in late July, merged with two others, burning a total of around 80,000 hectares (200,000 acres), making it the biggest blaze Spain has ever registered.

It consumed more than two-thirds of Izquierdo's land and killed 12 of his 85 cows. Another eight animals had to be put down because of their injuries. All the hay he had gathered to feed his cows in the winter was also burned.

"For us farmers, the summers are becoming more and more worrying, because they are getting hotter," he says. "It rains less, the wet season ends earlier and the autumn starts much later."

For farmers, such conditions are synonymous with fires.

"If you don't think about the wildfires too much, you feel okay," Izquierdo says. "But when a fire starts in a nearby village you start wondering – 'and what if we're next?'."

Wildfires are one of several symptoms of climate change which in recent years have had a substantial impact on Spain's economy, as well as contributing to shocking human tragedies.

World Weather Attribution, an international research organisation, found that the extreme conditions that drove record-breaking fires in Spain and Portugal in 2025 were 40 times more likely to happen due to the warming climate.

"The ultimate reason for the greater frequency and intensity of these kinds of fires has to be attributed to the increase in greenhouse gases caused mainly by the generalised use of fossil fuels," said Ernesto Rodríguez Camino, president of the Spanish Meteorology Association.

The Socialist Prime Minister, Pedro Sánchez, has described the fires in dramatic terms, placing Spain in the front line of an environmental crisis.

"The climate emergency kills," he said in July, during a visit to the southern province of Almería where a wildfire claimed 15 lives.

This year, around 300,000 hectares of land have been burned in Spain, according to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS), approximately half the total affected in the entire European Union.

In the last 40 years, damage caused by Spanish fires each year has exceeded 200,000 hectares on eight occasions – three of those since 2022.

'This landscape is completely charred': Inside the village at epicentre of Spain's wildfires

'It's a hell of a situation': Spain grapples with devastating wildfires

Farming insurance association Agroseguro estimated that 16,000 hectares of crops had been destroyed by mid-August this year, a major blow for Spain's agri-food industry, which contributes 9% of the country's GDP.

The local authorities in Castilla y León, the region most heavily affected by this year's massive fire near Madrid, are offering compensation – between €5,500 ($6,300; £4,700) and €25,000 ($29,000; £21,000) to each farmer – depending on the damage suffered. But Izquierdo estimates that this will cover less than half of his losses.

For decades, Spain's warm climate has been a boon for one of its other biggest industries - tourism. Sun-drenched resorts along the Mediterranean coast, and in the Balearic and Canary Islands, have driven the country's growth as a tourist hub.

This year, close to 100 million foreigners are expected to come to Spain, making it the second most-visited country in the world, just behind France.

Yet there are signs that the heat is becoming too much for some travellers. A study by researchers at Madrid's Rey Juan Carlos University found that it can as a deterrent to potential visitors.

"When there is a heatwave, the number of overnight stays drops in the destinations that we've studied, and there is also a drop in arrivals from some of Spain's biggest markets," says María Dolores Sánchez, an economist who co-authored the report.

"Tourism represents 13% of Spain's GDP, so this could have repercussions in the medium term when it comes to Spain's competitivity."

The medieval city of Toledo is on the plains of Castilla-La Mancha, far from Spain's coastline, but its rich history and winding streets have made it a popular destination for those seeking an alternative to the country's beaches and bars.

However, this summer tested their tolerance of heat, with the country registering a record-breaking 61 days of heatwaves that continued into early September. Toledo repeatedly saw temperatures in excess of 40C.

"It's quite difficult to do the tours in the summer," says guide Diego Esteban, of the company Visit Toledo. "We need to adapt, whether it is those of us who work in the tourism industry or the locals."

When leading tours in the summer months, Esteban makes sure that there are frequent stops, drinking water is provided and that the itineraries include plenty of shade. However, he would like to see more shade and drinking fountains available.

He says the heat has started to change the timing of the tourist season, bringing many more visitors during the cooler months of spring and autumn.

Warmer summers have also encouraged the so-called "coolcation" trend, whereby Spanish travellers seek out cooler areas to spend their holidays, typically in the north of the country.

Another consequence of Spain's warming climate has been drought. In 2024, after three years of minimal rainfall, the north-eastern region of Catalonia temporarily introduced stringent restrictions on water use, including a 25% reduction for industry and an 80% reduction for crop farming.

Heavy rainfall since then has lifted the restrictions, but the drought had a major impact on the local economy.

The most dramatic and tragic natural phenomenon Spain has seen in recent years were flash floods that killed 237 people in the east of the country in October 2024, centred on the Valencia region.

Spanish meteorological research group Climatoc-Lab described it as "a manifestation of how global warming alters the hydrological cycle".

The Valencia Chamber of Commerce estimated that the floods caused €4.5bn in direct damage. Thousands of businesses were affected, some literally washed away by the floodwater, while others were able to resume operations after a lengthy recovery.

"It was a disaster, both in terms of the lives lost and the impact on businesses, on workers, employers and ordinary people," says Laura Llácer Álvarez, manager of the Fepeval federation of industrial parks in the Valencia region.

Spain's geographical position, along with its climate and topography, make it unusually vulnerable as global temperatures increase. Germanwatch, an independent environmental organisation, ranked Spain the world's 20th most affected country in its climate risk index for 2024, just behind Nigeria and Mali.

Yet there are those who see an upside for the economy.

"Climate change affects how we produce, how we invest and how we consume," says Julián Cubero, head of economics of climate change at economic think tank BBVA Research. He points to how heat can act as a drag on economic activity.

"We all work worse when it's hot," he says. However, he adds, a greener economy can create new jobs with greater productivity.

"The key is to realise that if we don't act, growth will slow down, and if it's handled right it can become an opportunity," he says.

articles.title: In 2019, French runner Marie Leautey left Portugal to run around the world; 825 days and more than 28,000 km later, she set the women’s circumnavigation record at the time
articles.summary: US News: Marie Leautey was working as a finance executive in Singapore in 2017 when the idea first appeared on paper. She doodled a figure running around a glo.
articles.body: Marie Leautey was working as a finance executive in Singapore in 2017 when the idea first appeared on paper. She doodled a figure running around a globe during a conference call, and then looked into whether anyone had actually run around the world and began planning her own attempt. Two years later, on December 6, 2019, the French runner started from Cabo da Roca in Portugal. She would eventually cross four continents, cover 28,249 kilometres and spend 825 days to complete a route that is recognised by the World Runners Association (WRA). The association lists her as the holder of the women’s record for the fastest circumnavigation of Earth on foot.The idea began as a conference-call doodleA profile of her journey describes her as a former finance director who had built up her running gradually before deciding to attempt a world run. She spent roughly two years preparing for the journey, which included working out the rules, route, equipment and logistics. The WRA requires a recognised world run to cross four continents from ocean to ocean and to cover at least 26,232 kilometres on foot, and her eventual route exceeded that minimum by more than 2,000 kilometres.The WRA records 15,420 kilometres across Europe, 5,340 kilometres across North America, 3,002 kilometres across South America and 4,484 kilometres across Australia, which was followed by the final stretch in New Zealand. She started in Portugal and eventually finished at the Sydney Opera House on September 1, 2022. The run took place across the COVID-19 pandemic, which interrupted her original plans and forced changes to the journey.Leautey pushed a stroller that carried her equipment rather than travelling with a large support crew. Her setup was designed around self-sufficiency, and the route required her to manage food, water, camping and other supplies over long distances. The journey included mountains, deserts and long isolated roads rather than a continuous sequence of conventional city marathons.Nearly 700 marathons across four continentsLeautey had been running for more than two years by the time she returned to Europe after the long Australian leg. A September 2022 report in French newspaper Le Parisien said that her WRA-ratified journey covered about 28,300 kilometres in 825 days and involved the equivalent of hundreds of marathon distances. It also recorded her as the only woman at the time to have crossed four continents from ocean to ocean on foot under the organisation's criteria.Leautey generally ran six days a week, which covered roughly a marathon each running day. She crossed the Andes in South America, travelled through North America and later faced the huge distances between resupply points in Australia. Her equipment had to remain manageable because she was pushing it herself for much of the route.Border restrictions and changing travel rules affected her movement between countries, which forced adjustments to the original route. The WRA eventually ratified the completed circumnavigation despite the disruption.The record and what happened afterThe World Runners Association currently lists Leautey's 825-day, 28,249-kilometre journey as the women's fastest circumnavigation of Earth on foot, and its records page shows her record was established on September 1, 2022. The same page now lists Swiss runner Andrea Prais as the current women's record holder, after a 554-day circumnavigation completed in June 2026. That means Leautey's run remains part of the history of the women's record but is no longer the current record.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
