articles.title: New York rebuilt Belmont Park for $555 million after closing it for three years; the new grandstand is one-fifth the old size, four tracks are new and year-round racing is coming for the first time
articles.summary: US News: New York has reopened Belmont Park after a $555 million, three-year reconstruction that turned the historic Long Island racetrack into a modern sports.
articles.body: New York has reopened Belmont Park after a $555 million, three-year reconstruction that turned the historic Long Island racetrack into a modern sports and entertainment destination. The new five-story grandstand is about one-fifth the size of the old structure, freeing up space for green areas and public access to the infield, while four brand new racing surfaces will allow year-round racing at Belmont for the first time. Governor Kathy Hochul cut the ribbon on September 18, 2026, welcoming fans back to a venue that will host the return of the Belmont Stakes and the 2027 Breeders' Cup, according to the governor's office and local media coverage.A smaller grandstand with a bigger experienceThe most visible change at Belmont Park is the grandstand. The original building, which opened in the mid-20th century, had grown dated and inefficient, with vast interior spaces that were expensive to maintain and often underused. The new structure, designed by sports architecture firm Populous, covers roughly 300,000 square feet across five stories, down from about 1.25 million to 1.5 million square feet in the past. That reduction was intentional, aimed at creating a more intimate, fan-focused environment while unlocking land for parks, walking paths and gathering spaces.Inside, the design emphasises sightlines and connection to the action. Floor-to-ceiling windows give views of both the track and the paddock, and horses move to post through a glass-lined opening so spectators can see them up close. The first floor holds general-admission bars and concessions, while upper levels feature sit-down restaurants, clubs and a NYRA Bets room. Celebrity chef Marc Forgione is behind several dining concepts, including the Turf Club, with menus that range from chili lobster on Texas toast to steaks with bone marrow gremolata.Only the first two floors are open for the 2026 fall meet, with a capacity of around 6,000 for opening weekend. Floors three through five, including luxury suites and an event space with views toward the Manhattan skyline, are scheduled to be completed in early 2027, ahead of the Belmont Stakes return in June. When fully finished, the venue is expected to accommodate at least 50,000 spectators for major race days, matching the capacity of Saratoga Race Course.Four new tracks and the promise of year-round racingBeyond the grandstand, the racing surfaces themselves have been completely rebuilt. NYRA constructed four new tracks, including the traditional 1½-mile dirt oval that defines Belmont's identity, two turf courses and a one-mile synthetic Tapeta oval. The synthetic track is a key innovation, allowing racing to continue during winter months when dirt and turf conditions can be unreliable in the Northeast. For the first time in Belmont Park's history, this means the facility can host live racing year-round.These upgrades are not just about convenience. They are also about safety and consistency. Modern surfaces can be engineered to provide more uniform footing, reducing the risk of injuries to horses and jockeys. Multiple track options give race planners flexibility to match conditions to different types of races and to keep horses training and competing even when weather would previously have forced cancellations, as per reports.Economic impact and jobsA $455 million state loan secured by Governor Hochul in the fiscal year 2024 budget made the reconstruction possible, with total project costs reaching $555 million when track work and other improvements are included, reports share. During construction, the project created more than 3,700 union jobs and generated over $1 billion in economic activity, according to state officials. Once fully operational, Belmont Park is expected to produce about $155 million in annual economic output and roughly $10 million in new state and local tax revenue.Horse racing already supports an estimated $3 billion in annual economic activity across New York State and nearly 20,000 jobs. The return of Belmont, combined with the continued strength of Saratoga, gives New York both the oldest continuously operated thoroughbred racetrack in the country and one of the newest major racing venues built in the United States in more than four decades. For Long Island, the reopening is seen as a boost to hospitality, tourism and local businesses that depend on event-day traffic.Life on the backstretchThe redevelopment also targeted the backstretch, where trainers, grooms, exercise riders and other workers live and work during the racing season. NYRA completed two new dormitories since 2023, with a third due in fall 2026, adding modern housing for the backstretch community. Other investments include upgrades to the on-site medical clinic, a new Blue Light security system, renovations to the Recreation Hall and Track Kitchen, a refreshed gymnasium, improved flood mitigation and reliable Wi-Fi access.These changes respond to long-standing concerns about quality of life for the people who care for the horses. State officials and racing leaders describe the backstretch improvements as a core part of the project, not an afterthought. By investing in housing, safety and amenities, they hope to make Belmont a more attractive place for trainers and workers to base their operations, which in turn supports the overall health of the racing ecosystem.Major races return to Long IslandBelmont Park's closure in 2023 meant the Belmont Stakes, one of American racing's Triple Crown events, was temporarily moved to Saratoga Race Course. The new venue will welcome the Belmont Stakes back to its historic Long Island home in 2027, with the full grandstand expected to be ready in time. Last May, Governor Hochul also announced that Belmont would host the 2027 Breeders' Cup World Championships, marking the first time the year-end mega event has returned to New York since 2005.The 2026 fall meet, which began with a sold-out opening card of nine races headlined by the Grade 1, $1 million Jockey Club Gold Cup, runs for 46 days through December 6, generally from Thursday to Sunday. Advance general admission for most dates is priced at $7, or $10 at the gate. The Long Island Rail Road serves the Elmont–UBS Arena station, with complimentary shuttles running to the track on race days, making it easier for fans from across the region to attend without driving.A new chapter for an old iconBelmont Park first opened in 1905 and has long been synonymous with American thoroughbred racing. Its 1½-mile dirt track is known as the "Test of the Champion" because of the Belmont Stakes, which challenges horses with the longest distance of the Triple Crown. Over more than a century, the venue has hosted countless memorable moments, from Secretariat's record-setting performances to generations of champions who defined their eras on the big track.The 2026 reopening does not erase that history. A 200-year-old Japanese white pine that inspired Belmont's logo was preserved during construction, standing as a living link between the old and new eras. What has changed is the way fans experience the sport. The compact grandstand, expanded paddock, accessible infield and multiple dining and entertainment options are designed to encourage wandering, socialising and closer interaction with the horses, rather than sitting passively in stadium-style seats all afternoon.For racing fans, the promise of year-round racing, a modernised backstretch and the return of marquee events signals a fresh start for Belmont Park. For New York State, the project is both an economic investment and a statement about the place of horse racing in the state's cultural and tourism landscape. As the first new major racing venue built in the nation in more than 40 years, the new Belmont Park is positioned to shape how a new generation experiences the sport while honouring the legacy of one of its most iconic stages.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Mass casualty' alert? Pakistan hospitals clear beds ahead of PTI protest
articles.summary: Pakistan News: Hospitals in Islamabad have allegedly been ordered to prepare for a possible “humanitarian crisis” and “mass casualty incident” ahead of a planned Sep.
articles.body: Hospitals in Islamabad have allegedly been ordered to prepare for a possible “humanitarian crisis” and “mass casualty incident” ahead of a planned September 27 protest by jailed former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan’s party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).The instructions to Islamabad hospitals called for all scheduled elective surgeries to be postponed indefinitely and surgical departments to be prepared for a possible surge in patients, according to documents reviewed by Drop Site.Medical and support staff were ordered to remain available, with all forms of leave suspended. Hospitals were also told to recall employees who were already on leave.The measures were issued ahead of PTI’s planned September 27 march, which the party says is intended to demand Khan’s release.The preparations have already affected patients. People familiar with the situation told Drop Site that patients scheduled for surgery on Monday were informed that their procedures would be postponed.The government has not publicly said that the hospital preparations are specifically linked to a crackdown on PTI protesters. The documents, however, explicitly refer to preparations for a potential “humanitarian crisis” and “mass casualty incident”.Imran Khan's family detainedThe hospital preparations also came as authorities detained Khan’s three sisters – Aleema Khan, Noreen Niazi and Dr Uzma Khan – along with other members of his family, while several PTI leaders and workers were also arrested ahead of the planned march on Islamabad.Eight members of Khan’s family were reportedly detained within 24 hours. The children were later released after several hours, according to Aleema Khan’s son Shershah Khan, while Khan’s sisters remained in custody.Aleema Khan was detained under Section 3 of Pakistan’s Maintenance of Public Order law, with a formal order issued by Lahore’s deputy commissioner authorising her detention for 30 days, according to documents obtained by Drop Site.Similar detention orders circulated for Noreen Niazi and Uzma Khan.The arrests came after authorities stepped up action against PTI members ahead of the September 27 mobilisation. PTI has alleged that party offices were raided and elected representatives and workers were detained across the country.The arrests have come amid continuing concerns from Khan’s family and supporters over his health and prison conditions.Khan’s primary healthcare provider, Dr Faisal Sultan, has reportedly not been allowed to visit him for several weeks. Khan has been imprisoned since August 2023 after his government was removed from office following a no-confidence vote. PTI has continued to demand his release.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Sir Jim Ratcliffe suspends production at key UK plants blaming high gas prices
articles.summary: Ineos said natural gas in the UK is twelve times more expensive than in the US.
articles.body:
Billionaire Sir Jim Ratcliffe's industrial giant Ineos is pausing production at its three plants in Hull, blaming high UK gas prices.

The firm said gas prices in the UK are twelve times higher than in the US, and eight times more expensive than the coal-based processes used by Chinese competitors.

Sir Jim said: "We are being forced to mothball some of the most efficient plants in Europe, but with gas prices now 12 times the level in the US and 8 times that of China, we just cannot compete."

The facilities produce raw materials used to make pharmaceuticals, clothing, cosmetics, detergents, construction materials and military explosives in the UK and Europe. Gas is a key ingredient in production.

Ineos said the move will affect up to 1,000 of its staff, of whom 245 work directly at the site.

But the BBC understands workers across the sites will be kept on while Ineos tries to buy liquefied natural gas (LNG) directly from the US at lower prices - which could take up to a year - or waits for gas prices to go down.

Ineos is asking governments in the UK and the EU — where most of its products are exported to — to put in tariff protections against Chinese products.

One plant makes acetic acid, which is used in vinegar, paint and glue. Another makes acetic anhydride, a key ingredient of aspirin, and the third makes ethyl acetate, which is used as a solvent and for decaffeinating tea and coffee.

He said the current government's energy policy was "economic vandalism on an industrial scale".

The wholesale price of natural gas — used for heating homes and generating electricity — has almost doubled in the UK and Europe since July.

The disruption of supplies of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz following the US-Israel war in Iran has pushed up prices around the world.

Ineos says that its plants in Humberside are "among the most efficient in the world", producing materials with half the carbon footprint of US rivals, and only one eighth the footprint of Chinese equivalents.

Two plants are already shut and a third will stop production in the coming days, the company said.

It's the second time in less than a week that Sir Jim, who also owns a large stake in Manchester United, has heavily criticised government policy.

He told BBC News last week that he has lost confidence in the UK, describing the country as "on the slide", which he blamed on high taxes and high immigration.

Sir Jim, whose wealth is estimated to be around £15bn, has prompted controversy in the past with his comments on immigration. He was a supporter of Brexit but has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020.

The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade said it would be a "concerning time for workers in Saltend and their families".

A spokesperson said: "We've taken bold action to support our chemicals industry including £350 million for strategically important chemicals producers, which will be available on a co-investment basis.

"We've also put trade measures in place on foreign chemicals imports and are tackling high electricity costs via our Supercharger and British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme to keep our chemicals sector competitive."

articles.title: Brittany Ferries stops cross-Channel ferry route early
articles.summary: The ferry operator, which connects England with France and Spain, says it needs to "adapt".
articles.body:
A cross-Channel ferry route is to be shut down earlier than planned following a technical problem with a ship.

Brittany Ferries announced earlier this year that its last sailing between Portsmouth and Le Havre would be on 28 September.

It said an issue with the Commodore Clipper vessel meant it could no longer complete its final sailings. Travellers already booked can transfer to other crossings or get a full refund.

The company is ending the route, along with its Poole to Cherbourg service, due to financial challenges.

In a statement, the operator said: "We apologise to all affected customers, and are sorry that the route can't complete its final sailings; we know many had hoped to be part of them.

"It has been a pleasure for all at Brittany Ferries to link Portsmouth and Le Havre since 2013.

"However, the current economic context means the route is no longer viable and, sadly, we have had to make the difficult decision to close it."

Announcing the changes in June , the company said it faced a bill of €27m in 2026, which it blamed on rising taxes, Covid loan repayments, unfair competition and fewer travellers.

It said that although it had repaid half of its Covid support loan, significant debt remained, alongside new costs from the The European Union Emissions Trading System, despite major investments in greener ships.

Brittany Ferries insisted it would continue to offer a "comprehensive service" from Portsmouth, with regular sailings to Caen, Cherbourg and St Malo in France, to Guernsey in the Channel Islands, and to Santander and Bilbao in Spain.

articles.title: Gary Anderson: Sister's 'disbelief' Karol Kelly's killer released
articles.summary: Francesca Kelly says they were not told her brother's killer had been released from prison until after he absconded.
articles.body:
The sister of a man whose killer has been on the run for eight days has said her family had no idea he had been released from prison to attend his father's funeral until after he absconded.

Gary Anderson and his brother Sean were jailed for life in 2023 for the murder of Karol Kelly in Londonderry in 2018.

Anderson was freed from Maghaberry prison for two hours last Monday after a court sitting the previous day overturned a decision by the Northern Ireland Prison Service (NIPS) not to release him.

Francesca Kelly said the failings had been "at the highest level" and she wanted to raise these face-to-face with the Justice Minister Naomi Long.

Speaking for the first time since Anderson went on the run, Francesca said her family were only told about his release from prison in a phone call just before 14:00 BST on Monday, hours after it had happened, and after he had gone missing.

"At that stage the prisoner had already absconded for a few hours, so we weren't aware at all of any application for compassionate leave," she told BBC News NI.

"There was initially a sense of disbelief.

"I felt that maybe he would go missing for a few hours but eventually hand himself in.

"We certainly didn't think we would be sitting one week and a day later with him still at large."

She said the past eight days had taken a heavy toll on her family, describing it as "exhausting".

"You work hard to move forward in your life," she said. "You work hard to ensure the loved ones still here are okay and can move forward in their lives.

"But the trauma, it sits quietly within each and every one of us and it only takes one slight trigger, and you're right back to that night, you're right back to that graveside, you're right back to that courtroom - and that's a very difficult place to be."

Francesca said the justice system had let a lot of people down, including Karol's five children, the wider family and the jury at the trial who listened to "thorough, onerous and sometimes difficult evidence".

"It has also let down those brave witnesses who took the stand to ensure that they could share what they'd seen and experienced that night," she said.

"So yes, that is all the justice system has let all of us down, because their one job was to ensure that the sentence imposed by Judge Babington was adhered to, and it has not."

Asked if she had a message for Anderson, Francesca said the family had decided they were "not going to give energy to either him or that".

"But for me personally, I just find there's a big difference between being free and having freedom," she said.

"And I don't think a life where you're constantly looking over your shoulder, where you're living on your nerves, where you're not able to integrate in society or with those you love, I don't call that being free."

She said she believed that in time, Anderson would be "returned to his cell".

"And I trust that once the consequences of this situation are laid bare, this may not have seemed like as good an idea."

The justice minister has apologised to the Kelly family and agreed to meet them to hear their concerns.

The circumstances surrounding Anderson's release have sparked a political row in Northern Ireland, with Long denying on Monday that she had misled the assembly over the matter.

She has now ordered an independent review into what happened and said she understood why it would be distressing for Karol Kelly's family that one of his killers remains on the run.

A day before the funeral last Monday, a judge granted Anderson a two-hour compassionate temporary release (CTR) from Maghaberry Prison to attend.

It came after the application was originally denied by prison officials.

His brother Sean had also applied for compassionate leave from a different prison, Magilligan, but the decision to deny that application was upheld by the judge.

The funeral service took place at St Mary's Church in the Creggan area of Derry last Monday morning.

Anderson was not given permission to attend cremation in Letterkenny, County Donegal, in the Republic of Ireland that afternoon.

At some stage on Monday morning, he absconded from his court-approved civilian chaperone.

Court documents show that the chaperone appointed by the court to accompany Anderson during his father's funeral is a relative of the prisoner.

He is identified in court documents as an uncle; there is no suggestion of wrongdoing on his part.

Policing and justice expert Danny Shaw described it as a "very unusual situation".

"I can't remember, certainly in the UK, ever there being a situation like that where someone's been allowed out for a funeral without a prison officer or police officer in close attendance," he said.

Questions were raised over the granting of Anderson's compassionate temporary release (CTR) following the publication of the full 15-page judgement from the judicial review of the Prison Service's decision.

The judgment found that the decision to refuse Anderson's request was based on inaccurate information about the risk he posed.

The decision had been taken by the duty governor at Maghaberry Prison.

In his judgment, Mr Justice Rooney found that an internal assessment of Anderson's likelihood of reoffending had been recorded at a higher level than the score held on the Prison Service's internal system.

A legal representative for the Prison Service told the court that the increased score had come from a colleague rather than the duty governor's personal knowledge.

When the system was checked, Anderson's score was 27, indicating a medium likelihood of reoffending, rather than 32, which had been recorded as a high likelihood in the decision letter.

The judge found that the duty governor "clearly took account of this incorrect information" when assessing the risks and considering whether the decision was proportionate.

There is a question mark about what happened after the judge knocked back the original decision.

According to the judgment, the judge invited the duty governor to reconsider the decision, but that offer was declined.

The judge described the decision not to review it as "somewhat surprising" and he granted Anderson temporary release subject to a number of conditions, finding that the Prison Service's decision was "flawed" and had taken into account "irrelevant and incorrect factors".

The judge said the failure to secure and take account of the correct risk assessment was unlawful.

However Long, whose department oversees the Prison Service, has said a procedural failing by the Departmental Solicitor's Office (DSO), meant prison officials were not told that the judge had offered them the chance to reconsider their decision not to release Anderson.

articles.title: SpiceJet ordered to pay Rs 85,816 after delays make family miss connecting flight
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: The Patna district consumer commission has directed SpiceJet to pay Rs 85,816 to a passenger after repeated delays caused him and his famil.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Patna district consumer commission has directed SpiceJet to pay Rs 85,816 to a passenger after repeated delays caused him and his family to miss a connecting flight and incur hotel, transport and fresh air-ticket expenses. The commission also awarded 12 percent annual interest on Rs 15,816 and the order was passed on September 8, 2026.Why did the passenger approach the consumer commission?According to the commission order, Dilip Kumar Agarwal had booked three confirmed tickets from Patna to Mangalore via Mumbai for January 16, 2021, for Rs 18,697. The Patna-Mumbai flight was repeatedly delayed, due to which Agarwal and his family missed their connecting flight to Mangalore.He alleged that no food or refreshments were provided during the prolonged wait and that SpiceJet did not make alternate arrangements for their onward journey. He said the family had to spend money on a hotel and transport in Mumbai and buy fresh tickets from another airline. He received a refund of only Rs 4,389.Agarwal sought Rs 3,34,242, including the refund, consequential expenses and compensation for mental agony.SpiceJet contended that the delay was caused by bad weather in Delhi and was beyond its control. It relied on its terms of carriage and said airlines were not liable for delays caused by extraordinary circumstances.It also said the refund for the Mumbai-Mangalore sector had been processed through the travel agent. It relied on DGCA rules relating to delays caused by meteorological conditions and termed the passenger’s claim exaggerated and unsupported by evidence.Why did the commission hold SpiceJet responsible?The bench of President Prem Ranjan Mishra and member Rajnish Kumar said Agarwal and his family had reached Patna airport on time and were issued boarding passes, but the flight was repeatedly delayed. It also found that the airline had failed to provide food or refreshments during the prolonged wait.The commission said SpiceJet could not produce any official letter to prove that bad weather had caused the delay.“The airline failed to provide food or refreshments during prolonged waiting, which is a clear violation of DGCA CAR obligations,” the commission said.It further found that the repeated delay resulted in the family missing the connecting flight and that SpiceJet had not arranged an alternate flight to Mangalore.“Due to repeatedly delaying of flight from Patna to Mumbai, Complainant & his family missed connecting flight from Mumbai to Mangalore. Since O.P didn’t arrange any alternate flight to reach Mangalore from Mumbai, Complainant was bound to purchase fresh ticket from Mumbai to Mangalore from any other Airlines after paying any cost to attend son’s Medical Counselling. Hence, it is clear cut case of deficiency in service by O.P and O-P is liable to reimburse the cost of flight ticket which was purchased by the Complainant from GoAir,” it further added.The commission also accepted the documentary evidence relating to the hotel, transport, GoAir tickets and loss of advance hotel booking at Mangalore.“Documentary proof of hotel bills, transport, GoAir tickets, and loss of advance booking of Hotel at Mangalore has been produced, These expenses are genuine and directly attributable to the airline’s failure to provide alternate arrangements,” the bench noted.The commission then directed SpiceJet to reimburse Rs 20,205 towards the hotel stay, transport, GoAir tickets and loss of the advance hotel booking, after deducting the Rs 4,389 already refunded. This left Rs 15,816 payable to Agarwal.It also awarded Rs 50,000 for mental agony and physical harassment and Rs 20,000 as litigation costs. The Rs 15,816 amount will carry 12 percent annual interest from April 19, 2021, the date of filing of the complaint, until payment.The commission gave SpiceJet three months to comply. If it fails to do so, the amount will carry 15 percent annual penal interest. Agarwal may also seek execution of the order, with SpiceJet liable to pay an additional Rs 10,000 as execution costs.What did the commission order?The Patna district consumer commission directed SpiceJet to:Pay Rs 15,816 towards the hotel, transport, fresh GoAir tickets and loss of advance hotel booking, after adjusting the Rs 4,389 already refunded.Pay 12 percent annual interest on Rs 15,816 from April 19, 2021, until the amount is paid.Pay Rs 50,000 as compensation for mental agony and physical harassment.Pay Rs 20,000 towards litigation costs.Comply with the order within three months of receiving or producing the order.Pay 15 percent annual penal interest on the amount if it fails to comply within the three-month period.Pay an additional Rs 10,000 towards execution costs if the passenger seeks execution of the order.

articles.title: Burnham to warn EU chief of 'damage' posed by Made in Europe scheme
articles.summary: The prime minister says he will raise his concerns when the meets the European Commission President in New York.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham has warned of the "collateral damage" posed by the EU's Made In Europe rules, ahead of a meeting later with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen during a UN summit in New York.

The proposals aim to curb the presence of Chinese companies in the EU by giving manufacturers inside the bloc priority for public contracts and subsidies.

Speaking on the flight to the US, Burnham also declined to rule out committing to rejoining the EU in Labour's next manifesto, saying it was an issue "for another day".

He said his "immediate priority" was to rebuild the relationship with the EU and reach "practical agreement that will further boost the British economy".

The Made In Europe scheme - formally called the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) - is yet to be finalised, but the UK government is concerned that plans to favour EU companies could harm British manufacturing.

Burnham said it could "affect British industry and supply chains" and that he would raise his concerns with von der Leyen during a meeting that is expected to take place on Tuesday at the UN's annual summit.

"We have considerable support among the member states for the position we are taking, because Europe's argument is not with us," he added.

"We both suffer the same effects as other countries, particularly steel and the issue it raises for the steel industry in Europe and in Britain.

"We are making the argument 'we are not your enemies here… we are not the problem'. Made in Europe is dealing with a different problem.

"We are making the argument that 'let's avoid collateral damage'."

Tensions over the Made in Europe policy have reportedly further delayed this year's planned EU-UK summit, which had already been postponed in the wake of Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister in July.

Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting

Watch: What to expect from the UN General Assembly

Ten years on, Brexit's economic impact is becoming clearer

Burnham told reporters his own speech to the UN General Assembly later would reflect on the decade since the Brexit vote and the "turbulence comes when outside actors seek to manipulate, to distort facts, influence the British democratic process".

"Going into the next decade, we need to be clear-eyed about that and become stronger and more on the front foot about challenging that," he said.

Asked if he would rule out making a pledge to rejoin the EU at the next general election, Burnham said: "Our focus at the moment is on a UK-EU summit which we hope will take place later this year.

"My immediate priority is to build on the good work that Keir [Starmer] did in rebuilding bridges, because those bridges were broken in the early part of this decade."

He added: "What we have got to do is now go to the next level in terms of reaching practical agreement that will further boost the British economy, and those issues are the substance of the summit alongside EU requests around youth mobility."

He said questions about rejoining the EU were for "another day".

Speaking at the Liberal Democrat conference in Brighton on Monday, the EU's new ambassador to the UK was asked whether the UK could rejoin the EU or be granted associate membership.

Jukka Salovaara said: "The doors are open but it's very much up to the UK public to identify and decide on its level of ambition when it comes to deepening cooperation with the EU."

Last September, Burnham said he would like to see the UK back in the EU in his lifetime.

Earlier this year, he said Brexit had been "damaging" but "the last thing we should do right now is re-run those arguments".

The EU has recently suggested Canada could become the bloc's first "associate member".

Asked if this could be an option for the UK, Burnham said: "The European Union made it clear that that wasn't open to us."

articles.title: A school principal brought Chinese gooseberry seeds from China in 1904; 122 years later, New Zealand forecasts record kiwifruit production
articles.summary: Rest of World News: New Zealand’s kiwifruit story dates back to 1904, when Mary Isabel Fraser, a school principal, brought Chinese gooseberry seeds home from China. She g.
articles.body: New Zealand’s kiwifruit story dates back to 1904, when Mary Isabel Fraser, a school principal, brought Chinese gooseberry seeds home from China. She gave the seeds to Whanganui farmer Alexander Allison, who planted them in 1905; the vines produced their first fruit by 1910. According to a February 2026 report from the US Department of Agriculture’s Foreign Agricultural Service, the fruit was initially known as the ‘Chinese gooseberry’ before New Zealand exporters renamed it ‘kiwifruit’ in 1959 for the United States market. More than a century after Fraser brought the seeds to New Zealand, the country has become the world’s largest kiwifruit exporter.How a school principal in 1904 helped bring Chinese gooseberries to New ZealandIn 1904, Mary Isabel Fraser, a school principal, brought Chinese gooseberry seeds from China and gave them to a farmer, who planted them near Whanganui, which a USDA report described as the beginning of New Zealand’s kiwifruit history. The vines produced their first fruit in 1910. Around the same period, the species was also being tested as a commercial crop in the United Kingdom and the United States, but those attempts were largely unsuccessful in producing fruit. The report says kiwifruit vines grow best in frost-free environments with substantial water and protection from strong winds. Fraser’s seeds became the starting point for its later export industry.The Chinese gooseberry that became New Zealand’s global kiwifruitThe fruit grown from Fraser’s seeds was originally known as the Chinese gooseberry. During the Second World War, US troops stationed in New Zealand developed a taste for the fruit, which helped to increase interest in it. In 1959, New Zealand exporters renamed it ‘Kiwifruit’ for the United States market. According to the USDA report, the new name helped avoid Cold War associations and increased scrutiny linked to the term Chinese gooseberry. The name was derived from the kiwi, New Zealand’s national bird. The fruit later became a major export crop. New Zealand is now the world’s second-largest kiwifruit producer and accounts for more than 65% of global kiwifruit exports across several international markets.How did New Zealand’s kiwifruit industry become a major horticulture sectorNew Zealand’s kiwifruit industry is now the largest sector in the country’s horticulture industry, according to the report. More than 2,800 growers cultivate kiwifruit across about 14,500 hectares of orchards. The Bay of Plenty is the main production region, accounting for about 79% of total output. The industry has also recovered from PSA (Pseudomonas Syringae pv. Actinidiae), a bacterial disease detected in New Zealand in 2010 that caused widespread and severe damage to vines. Gold kiwifruit varieties, which are more tolerant to present PSA strains, helped the sector recover. Zespri serves as the central marketer, export agent and global distribution lead for almost all New Zealand kiwifruit exports under the country’s Single Point of Entry model for its exports to international markets worldwide.New Zealand’s kiwifruit exports hit a record as production risesThe USDA’s Foreign Agricultural Service forecasts New Zealand’s kiwifruit production at 800,000 metric tons in the 2025/2026 market year, almost 1% higher than the previous year. If achieved, this would be the country’s highest production level on record. The report attributes the expected increase to maturing SunGold and RubyRed orchards, greater seasonal labour availability and favourable weather conditions. In 2024/2025, production was estimated at 794,490 metric tons, while exports increased 44% to almost 767,620 metric tons, marking the largest export year to date. The European Union was the largest market, accounting for 32% of exports, followed by China at 27%, Japan at 14%, and the United States at 6%.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
